# Physical Goods

`customer_support.offering.product.physical_goods` · offering_type · parent `customer_support.offering.product`

> Goods that are picked, shipped, held and consumed. It differs from hardware in that the item is not diagnosed, it is replaced — nobody troubleshoots a jumper — and it differs from every other offering in this tree in that most contacts are not about the product at all. "Where is my order" is the dominant intent by a wide margin, and it is a question about a carrier's network, answered out of a tracking system we do not own, concerning an exception we did not cause and cannot correct. That is the worst structural position support can occupy: we own the relationship and none of the control. The customer holds us responsible, entirely correctly, because they bought from us and have never heard of the third party involved. Our only unilateral levers are reship and refund, and both cost goods rather than minutes, which is why cost-to-serve in this offering is measured in units and margin rather than in handle time. Volume is seasonal to the point of violence and is driven by events outside the company altogether — weather, a carrier disruption, a promotion, a peak trading week. Capacity planned against an annual average is wrong on every single day of the year, in one direction or the other. The habit to unlearn on arrival from software support is waiting for certainty before answering. A stalled delivery scan has no diagnosis coming; the information the carrier will give us in four days is already the information we have now, and a proactive message sent the hour the scan stops deflects more contacts than any article ever written for this business.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| delivery | picked, packed and carried to an address by a third party we contract but do not control |
| pricing_shape | one-off transactional purchase, frequently low value, sometimes a replenishment subscription |
| margin_profile | thin unit margin — a single reship or refund erases the margin on several other orders, which means an agent choosing between waiting, reshipping and refunding is making a direct P&L decision in about ninety seconds with no finance training |
| post_sale_load | concentrated in the delivery window and then again in the returns window, with almost nothing in between |
| support_load | dominated by order status and delivery exceptions rather than product faults. Violently seasonal, with peak weeks running at several times baseline, and spiky on inputs nobody in the company scheduled: weather, carrier failures, and our own marketing |
| resolution_locus | a warehouse, a carrier or the refund ledger — third parties whose relationship we own and whose behaviour we cannot influence inside the life of one ticket. Where the goods themselves are faulty the locus is a supplier, which is slower still and equally out of reach |
| notes | Returns are a second support motion hiding inside this one. They have their own clock, their own fraud surface and their own emotional register, and organisations that route them into the ordinary queue discover that a return conversation and a delivery conversation need opposite defaults about giving the customer the benefit of the doubt.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `intent_ref`, `external_ref`


> `external_ref` is the order number, and a contact without one cannot be answered at all — which makes capturing it an intake problem rather than a triage problem, and moves the cost of missing it to the very front of the queue. `intent_ref` matters because an order-status contact is not a support case: putting a diagnostic workflow on a logistics question wastes the agent's time and reads to the customer as evasion.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.customer_sentiment`

Requires `broken_promise_count`, `trajectory`


> Delivery promises are made in public, dated, and broken visibly. Sentiment in this offering is almost entirely a function of how many times a stated date has moved, not of how the messages were worded, and a sentiment read that ignores the promise ledger will keep scoring a polite third apology as a neutral conversation.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.commitment`


> Worth noting even though the object is not authored yet: the commitment in this offering is frequently one we did not make. A carrier's estimated delivery date is quoted to the customer by our own storefront, becomes a promise in their mind, and is then missed by somebody else. Any commitment model here needs to distinguish a promise we control from a promise we merely displayed.
